summary:
FINAL ORBIT is a story-driven browser game for the Space Mission Design Game challenge. You play the chief engineer of Astra Dynamics, a small space company that lost its first rocket after you cleared it for launch with an unresolved avionics warning. Now you have to decide what to test, what to fix, and when you have enough evidence to fly. A test can uncover a defect. Fixing it takes time and money, and removing the affected hardware can cost you a capability you were counting on.

Lead your crew through three missions of rising difficulty: a CubeSat that must deliver Earth observations to a ground team, an orbital rocket demonstration, and an uncrewed lunar science lander. From feasibility through launch and operations, you choose the orbit, instruments, and backups while balancing mass, power, data, budget, and schedule.
details:
What it does. FINAL ORBIT lets players design, manage and fly a complete space mission. The story starts with a failed launch: two years ago the player signed a launch release while an avionics warning was still open, and the rocket was lost. The company now has one last chance, and every chapter asks the player to do better.

How it works.

  • Three missions unlock in order: CubeSat (easy), orbital launch (medium) and lunar mission (hard).
  • Each mission follows NASA's life cycle phases and reviews (MDR, PDR, CDR, FRR). The crew (a project manager, a systems engineer and a client contact) explains each phase in plain language.
  • Players compare designs in crew meetings. In the CubeSat mission they pick a client, a launch and orbit (ISS deployment at 420 km, 51.6°, or a rideshare to a 550 km sun-synchronous orbit) and observation capability. Every option shows mass, peak power, first-pass data, schedule and cost before the player commits.
  • Hidden defects vary with the mission seed. In the CubeSat mission, a backup sensor can help recover observations when the main instrument’s view is obstructed. If integration testing finds an interface fault, the sensor must be repaired or removed before flight clearance. Repairing and retesting takes more time and budget. Removing the sensor and retesting is quicker, but leaves the mission without that backup. In missions where a waiver is available, players can also choose to fly with a known risk.
  • The flight simulation shows what reached the ground, and the results page rates mission success, science value, resource use and engineering judgement. Players can replay the same seed to compare strategies.
  • The orbital mission adds target orbit, upper stage, telemetry, payload adapter, ground stations, hot-fire testing and a funding cut. The lunar mission adds partner offers, the route to the Moon, backup sensors, propellant margin and event cards based on 30 real mission cases.

Benefits and intended impact. Students rarely get to run a whole mission. FINAL ORBIT turns abstract trade-offs into choices with visible consequences, and shows that verification is about knowing the truth before launch. It runs in any browser, needs no install, and is available in English and Traditional Chinese.

Tools. TypeScript, React, Vite, Playwright and Node's test runner (94 unit tests and 23 browser tests), GitHub Pages.

Creativity and design considerations. A redemption story gives the player a personal reason to verify. Pixel-art scenes show the crew at work, on the launch pad and in mission control. Launch scenarios use representative orbital parameters. Costs, schedules, power budgets, and downlink capacity are simplified for gameplay.
